subject: physiology
title: Erlanger-Gasser Nerve Fibre Classification and Conduction

steps.tx: Mammalian peripheral nerve trunks contain heterogeneous populations of axons subserving distinct motor, sensory, and autonomic functions. The classical **Erlanger-Gasser classification** categorizes peripheral nerve fibres into three major groups designated A, B, and C based on axonal diameter, degree of myelination, and compound action potential conduction velocity.
steps.say: The Erlanger-Gasser classification divides peripheral nerve axons into groups A, B, and C based on diameter, myelination, and conduction speed.

steps.tx: The largest and fastest fibres belong to the myelinated **A-alpha fibre** class. Measuring twelve to twenty micrometres in diameter, they conduct action potentials at rapid velocities between seventy and one hundred and twenty metres per second. Functionally, A-alpha fibres encompass alpha motor neurons supplying extrafusal skeletal muscle and primary afferents from muscle spindle annulospiral endings.
steps.say: A-alpha fibres are the largest myelinated axons, conducting up to 120 metres per second to serve somatic motor units and muscle spindle afferents.

steps.tx: Tactile and mechanoreceptive sensations travel through A-beta fibres, whereas acute sharp nociception is mediated by **A-delta fibres**. These thinly myelinated axons transmit fast, pricking, well-localized first pain, cold thermal sensations, and light mechanical stimuli at velocities of twelve to thirty metres per second, terminating in lamina I and V of the spinal dorsal horn.
steps.say: A-delta fibres are thinly myelinated axons that transmit sharp, localized first pain and cold temperature into dorsal horn laminae.

steps.tx: In contrast to myelinated axons, unmyelinated **C fibres** represent the smallest axons in peripheral nerves, measuring less than one point two micrometres. Conducting sluggishly between zero point five and two metres per second, C fibres transmit slow burning second pain, warm sensations, and postganglionic sympathetic autonomic outflow, embedded in Remak Schwann cell bundles.
steps.say: Unmyelinated C fibres conduct below two metres per second, carrying slow aching pain, warmth, and postganglionic sympathetic signals.

steps.tx: Axonal conduction velocity is governed by axon geometry and insulation. In myelinated fibres, **conduction velocity** scales linearly with external fibre diameter, following the Hursh factor where velocity in metres per second equals diameter in micrometres multiplied by approximately six. In unmyelinated fibres, conduction velocity increases proportionately only to the square root of axonal diameter.
steps.say: Conduction velocity scales linearly with diameter in myelinated fibres by the Hursh factor, but only with the square root of diameter in unmyelinated fibres.

steps.tx: Insulation of the axon by multilayered concentric wraps of Schwann cell membrane produces **myelination**. Myelin dramatically increases effective transmembrane electrical resistance while decreasing membrane capacitance up to fifty-fold. This electrical insulation prevents outward dissipation of local longitudinal currents across the internodal axonal membrane between adjacent nodes of Ranvier.
steps.say: Myelination wraps axons in Schwann cell membranes, dramatically increasing membrane resistance and lowering capacitance to prevent current leakage.

Depolarises Adjacent Node of Ranvier to Threshold

steps.tx: Because ionic current is barred from traversing insulated internodes, action potentials leap from one node of Ranvier to the next in **saltatory conduction**. Clusters of voltage-gated sodium channels exceeding one thousand per square micrometre at the nodal gap guarantee a safety factor of five, allowing instantaneous regenerative spiking across successive internodal intervals.
steps.say: Saltatory conduction forces action potentials to jump between nodes of Ranvier, accelerating conduction twenty-fold while conserving metabolic energy.

steps.tx: A parallel sensory classification scheme designates primary muscle and tendon afferents by Roman numerals. Group Ia fibres supply primary muscle spindle annulospiral endings, **Group Ib fibres** innervate Golgi tendon organs monitoring muscle tension, Group II fibres supply secondary spindle flower-spray endings, Group III matches A-delta fibres, and Group IV matches unmyelinated C fibres.
steps.say: The numerical sensory system classifies muscle afferents: Ia and II for muscle spindles, Ib for Golgi tendon organs, III for fast pain, and IV for unmyelinated fibres.
